profile.subject: Cleopatra
profile.overview: Cleopatra VII ruled Egypt at a time when Roman armies and politicians increasingly decided the fate of the Mediterranean. Through alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, she tried to preserve her kingdom, but her defeat and death in 30 BC brought Egypt under Roman rule.

key_moments.title: A throne shared with a brother
key_moments.text: When her father **Ptolemy XII** died, **Cleopatra** inherited the Egyptian throne alongside her younger brother **Ptolemy XIII**. Their joint reign became a struggle for power: the queen who had inherited a kingdom was eventually driven out of it.
claims: Cleopatra and Ptolemy XIII succeeded Ptolemy XII as rulers of Egypt in 51 BC.
Cleopatra and Ptolemy XIII became rivals for control of Egypt.
Cleopatra was driven from Egypt during the struggle with Ptolemy XIII.

key_moments.title: Caesar restores her rule
key_moments.text: **Julius Caesar** arrived in Egypt during Cleopatra’s struggle with her brother and backed her claim to power. Fighting in and around Alexandria ended with **Ptolemy XIII’s defeat and death**, and Cleopatra returned to the throne. Her new fellow ruler was another younger brother, **Ptolemy XIV**.
claims: Julius Caesar arrived in Egypt in 48 BC and supported Cleopatra in the dispute with Ptolemy XIII.
The Alexandrian war ended in 47 BC with the defeat and death of Ptolemy XIII.
Cleopatra subsequently ruled Egypt jointly with the younger brother Ptolemy XIV.

key_moments.title: A partnership with Antony
key_moments.text: Cleopatra met **Mark Antony** at Tarsus, beginning a political and personal partnership with one of Rome’s most powerful commanders. At the **Donations of Alexandria**, Antony publicly assigned territories and royal titles to Cleopatra and their children. He also recognized **Caesarion**, Cleopatra’s son, as Julius Caesar’s son—a challenge to **Octavian**, Caesar’s adopted heir.
claims: Cleopatra met the Roman commander Mark Antony at Tarsus in 41 BC and became Antony’s political ally and partner.
At the Donations of Alexandria in 34 BC, Mark Antony assigned territories and royal titles to Cleopatra and the children of Cleopatra and Mark Antony.
At the Donations of Alexandria, Mark Antony recognized Caesarion as Julius Caesar’s son.
Recognition of Caesarion as Julius Caesar’s son challenged the position of Octavian as Julius Caesar’s adopted heir.

key_moments.title: Defeat ends the kingdom
key_moments.text: The forces of **Octavian** defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the naval **Battle of Actium**. The following year, Octavian invaded Egypt; Antony and Cleopatra both died, and **Egypt became a Roman province**. Cleopatra’s attempt to keep her dynasty in power ended with Rome taking control of the kingdom itself.
claims: Octavian’s forces defeated the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BC.
Octavian invaded Egypt in 30 BC.
Mark Antony and Cleopatra died in 30 BC after Octavian invaded Egypt.
Following Cleopatra’s defeat and death, Egypt became a Roman province and Ptolemaic rule ended.

deep_facts.text: Cleopatra belonged to a dynasty whose court language was Greek, yet she could also speak Egyptian. Plutarch describes her moving between languages when speaking with foreign peoples, often without an interpreter. The ruler so often remembered through Roman stories was also someone who could address her Egyptian subjects in their own language.
claims: Greek was the court language of the Ptolemaic dynasty to which Cleopatra belonged.
Cleopatra spoke Egyptian.
Plutarch describes Cleopatra speaking several languages and communicating with many foreign peoples without an interpreter.

deep_facts.text: On an outer wall of the temple of Hathor at Dendera, Cleopatra appears with her son Caesarion in the visual language of Egyptian kingship. The relief places a queen from a Greek-speaking dynasty inside an ancient religious tradition: mother and son are shown presenting offerings to Egyptian gods.
claims: A relief on an outer wall of the temple of Hathor at Dendera depicts Cleopatra and Caesarion.
The Dendera relief depicts Cleopatra and Caesarion presenting offerings to Egyptian gods in Egyptian royal style.
Cleopatra belonged to the Greek-speaking Ptolemaic dynasty.

deep_facts.text: Cleopatra’s daughter Cleopatra Selene II survived the fall of her mother’s kingdom and was raised in the household of Octavia, Mark Antony’s Roman wife. Selene later married Juba II and became queen of Mauretania in North Africa. The daughter of Antony and Cleopatra thus grew up under the care of the woman Antony had married before his final break with Rome.
claims: Cleopatra Selene II was the daughter of Cleopatra and Mark Antony.
After the fall of Cleopatra’s kingdom, Cleopatra Selene II was raised in the household of Octavia, the Roman wife of Mark Antony.
Cleopatra Selene II married Juba II and became queen of Mauretania in North Africa.
Mark Antony married Octavia before the final conflict between Mark Antony and Octavian.

deep_facts.1.text: The full offering-and-Egyptian-kingship interpretation remains unsupported to the heightened corroboration standard. The Egyptian UNESCO nomination (https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/1824/) identifies Cleopatra and Caesarion on the exterior relief; the C. M. Dixon photograph catalogue identifies offerings to gods, but neither provides independent corroboration of the complete royal-style interpretation. Narrow the passage to “On an outer wall of the temple of Hathor at Dendera, a relief depicts Cleopatra with her son Caesarion. Cleopatra belonged to the Greek-speaking Ptolemaic dynasty.” Set its source to the fetched UNESCO nomination. This is an evidence gap, not a finding that the scene is false.

deep_facts.2.text: Selene’s upbringing in Octavia’s household is an obscure anecdote with one underlying original account: Plutarch, Life of Antony. The Wikipedia discussion and Bennett genealogy depend on that same account and cannot satisfy the two-independent-original-accounts rule. Remove the upbringing statement and the final sentence repeating it, retaining Selene’s parentage, survival, marriage to Juba II, and Mauretanian queenship. Alternatively, explicitly attribute the upbringing to Plutarch and verify the passage as an attributed account.

key_moments.2.text: “one of Rome’s most powerful commanders” is a superlative requiring two independent original accounts on distinct hosts. The evidence establishes Antony’s eastern command and includes one OCR educational account describing powerful Roman partners, but does not supply the required independent corroboration of this comparison. Replace the phrase with “a Roman commander”.

deep_facts.1.text: The full offering-and-Egyptian-kingship interpretation remains unsupported to the heightened corroboration standard. The Egyptian UNESCO nomination (https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/1824/) identifies Cleopatra and Caesarion on the exterior relief; the C. M. Dixon photograph catalogue identifies offerings to gods, but neither provides independent corroboration of the complete royal-style interpretation. Narrow the passage to “On an outer wall of the temple of Hathor at Dendera, a relief depicts Cleopatra with her son Caesarion. Cleopatra belonged to the Greek-speaking Ptolemaic dynasty.” Set its source to the fetched UNESCO nomination. This is an evidence gap, not a finding that the scene is false.

deep_facts.2.text: Selene’s upbringing in Octavia’s household is an obscure anecdote with one underlying original account: Plutarch, Life of Antony. The Wikipedia discussion and Bennett genealogy depend on that same account and cannot satisfy the two-independent-original-accounts rule. Remove the upbringing statement and the final sentence repeating it, retaining Selene’s parentage, survival, marriage to Juba II, and Mauretanian queenship. Alternatively, explicitly attribute the upbringing to Plutarch and verify the passage as an attributed account.
key_moments.2.text: unverifiable: Antony was one of Rome’s most powerful commanders.
deep_facts.2.text: unverifiable: Selene was raised in Octavia’s household after Egypt’s fall.
deep_facts.1.text: unverifiable: The Dendera relief depicts Cleopatra and Caesarion presenting offerings to Egyptian gods in traditional Egyptian royal style.
